StudentBook helps private tutors keep student contacts and tuition details in one place. It runs on your computer and uses typed commands.

This development branch supports student contacts, subjects, schooling levels, weekly lesson slots and hourly rates. You can add, view, edit and clear a subject, level, lesson slot or hourly rate, and find students by level. The app saves changes automatically. Separate guardian commands add, edit and remove one optional name and phone contact per student, displayed in the student list.
* Add, list, edit and delete student records.
* Record each student's subjects, schooling level, guardian contact, weekly lesson slot and hourly rate.
* Save records locally and reopen them later.
All five tuition features are part of the MVP. Payment processing and sending messages are out of scope. Other brainstormed ideas are backlog candidates, not promised additions.

This mock-up shows the planned MVP. The User Guide describes the commands available now. See the [Developer Guide](docs/DeveloperGuide.md#product-scope) for feature owners and decisions still to confirm.

Start with the [User Guide](docs/UserGuide.md) to use the app or the [Developer Guide](docs/DeveloperGuide.md) to contribute. The [project website](https://ay2627s1-cs2103t-f13-4.github.io/tp/) publishes the merged documentation.
For course milestones, weekly tasks, and release requirements, see the [TP planning guides](planning/README.md).
This project is based on the AddressBook-Level3 project created by the [SE-EDU initiative](https://se-education.org). It uses Java and JavaFX, with Gradle for building and testing.
We are a team based in the [School of Computing, National University of Singapore](https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg).

`StorageManager` delegates record files to `JsonAddressBookStorage` and preferences to `JsonUserPrefsStorage`. Both use JSON and convert stored values to model objects.

`Person` is an abstract base class holding a `Name` and `Phone`. `Student` and `Guardian` extend it. `isSamePerson` and `equals` compare the runtime class as well as the fields, so a student never equals a guardian. `UniquePersonList` only stores students, and two students are duplicates when their `Name` is exactly equal (case-sensitive).
A `Student` adds an `Email`, an `Address`, a set of `Tag`s and the tuition fields below. Optional fields use `Optional`; absence means "not recorded".
| Schooling level | `Optional<SchoolingLevel>` | One text label, 1 to 30 ASCII characters after the space cleanup below |
| Guardian | `Optional<Guardian>` | Both `Name` and `Phone`, using AB3 validation |
| Lessons | `List<Lesson>` | Zero or more lessons in insertion order; identical lessons are rejected |
A `Lesson` is an immutable value object:
| Subject | `Subject` | Required. 1 to 40 ASCII characters after the space cleanup below; equality ignores case |
| Weekly slot | `WeeklyLessonSlot` | Required. `DayOfWeek`, `LocalTime start` and `LocalTime end`; whole minutes, end later on the same day. Parsing ignores case |

| Hourly rate | `HourlyRate` | Required. SGD/hour as a non-negative `BigDecimal` with at most two decimal places, stored with scale 2; zero is a recorded value. `HourlyRate.isValidHourlyRate` holds the text rule |
| Location | `Optional<LessonLocation>` | 1 to 100 characters after space cleanup. A word of letters followed by `/` (such as `x/`) is rejected because it looks like a command prefix |
| Mode | `Optional<LessonMode>` | `PHYSICAL` or `VIRTUAL`, ignoring case and surrounding spaces |
Subject and level use text labels, not enums. For both:
* Remove leading and trailing spaces or tabs. Replace repeated spaces or tabs with one space. Keep uppercase and lowercase letters as entered.
* Start with an ASCII letter or digit and include at least one letter.
* Allow letters, digits, spaces, apostrophes, hyphens, periods and parentheses.
* Do not map synonyms or check whether a subject matches a level.

Lesson equality includes every field, including location and mode. Overlapping time slots are allowed. Siblings can have the same guardian details, but each student keeps a separate copy. There is no tutor/student role field or generic `class[]` field.
`Student` has two constructors. The five-argument form (`name, phone, email, address, tags`) leaves the level and guardian absent and the lesson list empty. The full form is:

All arguments, including each `Optional` and each lesson, must be non-null. The constructor throws `IllegalArgumentException` (`Student.MESSAGE_DUPLICATE_LESSONS`) if `lessons` contains duplicates, and `getLessons()` returns an unmodifiable list.
* Every edit keeps fields it does not change. `edit` cannot change lessons or the guardian; the `lesson-` and `guardian-` commands build a replacement `Student` and call `Model#setPerson`.
* Full equality and hashing include all tuition fields.
* Existing sample records may leave tuition fields absent.
Storage uses the configured file path, default `data/addressbook.json`, and the top-level `persons` array. `JsonAdaptedPerson` writes these properties in addition to the contact fields:
| `guardianContact` | Object with `name` and `phone` (the key keeps its original name so existing files still load) |
| `lessons` | Array of lesson objects; empty means no lessons |
Each lesson object, written by `JsonAdaptedLesson`, has:
| `weeklyLessonSlot` | Object with uppercase English `day`, such as `MONDAY`, and `start`/`end` in `HH:mm` |
| `location` | Text string; omitted when not recorded |

Missing or null `schoolingLevel`, `guardianContact` and `lessons` load as absent or empty. Supplied values must have the correct JSON type and pass the model validation; a lesson missing `subject`, `weeklyLessonSlot` or `hourlyRate` is rejected.

**Older data files:** files saved before lessons existed stored `subjects`, `weeklyLessonSlot` and `hourlyRate` directly on each student. There is no migration: Jackson ignores those unknown properties on load, and the next save removes them. This is acceptable while there are no real users. Delete or convert an old `data/addressbook.json` if you need to keep its tuition details.

Tests cover loading, save/reload and invalid values (`TuitionStorageTest`). A failed save reports an error but does not undo the in-memory change. A failed load does not block commands. These inherited failure behaviors differ from the earlier specification; see [decisions to confirm](#decisions-to-confirm).
`lesson-add`, `lesson-edit` and `lesson-delete` are routed by `AddressBookParser` to `LessonCommandParser`, parameterized by `LessonCommand.Operation`.

| Parse | `LessonCommandParser` rejects unknown and repeated prefixes, then validates each value with `ParserUtil` (`parseSubject`, `parseWeeklyLessonSlot`, `parseHourlyRate`, `parseLessonMode`, `parseLessonLocation`). Add requires subject, slot and rate; edit requires at least one field; delete takes none. An empty `mode/` or `location/` is valid only in `lesson-edit`, where it clears that field. |
| Execute | `LessonCommand` resolves the student from the current filtered list, copies the lesson list, then adds, replaces or removes one entry. Edit keeps any lesson field that was not supplied. |

| Validate | A result containing duplicate lessons fails with `MESSAGE_DUPLICATE_LESSON`. A bad student or lesson index fails with `MESSAGE_INVALID_PERSON_DISPLAYED_INDEX` or `MESSAGE_INVALID_LESSON_DISPLAYED_INDEX`. Failures leave the model unchanged. |
| Update | The command builds a replacement `Student` with the new lesson list and every other field copied, then calls `Model#setPerson`. The active filter stays. |

| Display | `PersonCard` shows `Lessons: Not recorded`, or one `- ` line per lesson using `Lesson#toString`, for example `Math, Wednesday 1.00pm-5.00pm, SGD 45.50/hour, Physical, at Clementi Library`. A lesson's number is its position in that list, starting from 1. |
| Save | `LogicManager` saves through the existing storage workflow; `JsonAdaptedLesson` persists each lesson. |

`GuardianCommandParser`, parameterized by the operation. The parser validates the displayed index and guardian

`GuardianCommand` resolves the student from the current filtered list. Adding an existing guardian, or editing or

The current filter remains active. Siblings can hold identical guardian contacts independently.

`GuardianWorkflowTest` covers CRUD, partial updates, filtered indices, invalid requests, siblings sharing a guardian,

Validation remains the current AB3 validation; broader name and phone rules remain a product decision.
Undo and redo are not implemented or part of the selected tuition work. The inherited AB3 proposal uses `VersionedAddressBook` to store snapshots and a pointer to the current snapshot.
* `commit()` adds a snapshot after a successful change and removes any redo history.
* `undo()` moves to the previous snapshot; `redo()` moves to the next.
* Failed commands and read-only commands do not add snapshots. Moving past either end reports an error.
* Full snapshots are simpler to implement but use more memory. Command-specific inverse operations use less memory but require correct undo logic for each command.
The inherited diagrams remain in `docs/diagrams` and `docs/images` for reference. Data archiving is also unimplemented.

These are acceptance targets. They have not all been verified in the current app.
1. **Compatibility.** Run on Windows, macOS and Linux with Java `25`, on systems supported by the bundled JavaFX runtime.

2. **Capacity and speed.** Support 1,000 students, each with one guardian. Adding, listing or deleting a record should show its result within two seconds. Test on a supported computer with at least 4 GB of RAM and local storage. Measure from command submission to the displayed result, excluding startup.
3. **Keyboard use.** After launch, let tutors add, list and delete students without a mouse.
4. **Error messages.** Explain what is wrong and how to fix it. Invalid input should leave existing records unchanged.
5. **Saved data.** After a successful save and normal shutdown, restore every contact and tuition field on restart, including implemented tuition fields. Users should not have to re-enter data.
6. **Offline use.** Manage and save records on the tutor's computer without internet access or an online account.

7. **Data protection.** Keep student and guardian contact details out of external services and diagnostic logs. The tutor's operating-system account and file permissions control access to local files.

8. **File errors.** Report file failures clearly. The intended recovery behavior still needs confirmation; see [decisions to confirm](#decisions-to-confirm). Valid AB3 files must load with new fields absent.
* **StudentBook**: The desktop app for managing student records.
* **Independent private tutor**: A tutor who manages students and lessons without administrative staff.
* **Student record**: One student's contact details, schooling level, guardian contact and lessons. Notes remain a backlog candidate.
* **Guardian contact**: The name and phone number of the adult responsible for a student. The first version allows one optional guardian per student. A recorded guardian needs both fields.
* **Schooling level**: The student's stage of primary or secondary education, such as Primary 5 or Secondary 3.
* **Subject**: An academic subject taught by the tutor to a student, such as Mathematics or English.
* **Lesson**: One recurring arrangement for a student: a subject, a weekly slot and an hourly rate, with an optional location and mode. A student can have many lessons.
* **Recurring lesson slot**: A lesson's weekly day, start time and end time on a single day.
* **Lesson mode**: Whether a lesson is physical or virtual.
* **Hourly rate**: The agreed SGD amount per hour for a lesson, stored as `BigDecimal`. It does not calculate fees or process payments.
* **Progress note**: A dated note recording a student's learning progress or observations from a lesson.
* **Guardian follow-up item**: A recorded action the tutor needs to carry out for a guardian, such as providing an update. An outstanding item has not yet been marked complete.
* **Displayed index**: The number beside a student in the current list. It can change when the list changes, so it is not a permanent student ID.
* **Local storage**: Files on the tutor's computer that keep records between launches.
* **Private contact detail**: A student or guardian's phone number, email address, or other contact information intended for the tutor's use rather than public sharing.

3. Run `find Alex`, then delete a valid result index. Check that it deletes that search result, not the record at the same position in the full list.

5. Run `lesson-edit INDEX 2 mode/ location/`. The card should show the English lesson without mode or location, including after restart.
6. Run `lesson-delete INDEX 1`. English becomes lesson 1. Delete it too and the card should show `Lessons: Not recorded`.

2. Run `guardian-edit INDEX phone/87654321`. The guardian's name should remain unchanged. Restart and verify persistence.
3. Run `guardian-edit INDEX name/John Tan`. The phone should remain unchanged.

6. Filter to one student with `find`, then use `guardian-add 1 name/Janet Tan phone/91234567`.
Check that only the displayed student changes, the filter remains active, and other students are untouched.
Close the app and back up the test data before each case.
* **Missing file:** Move `data/addressbook.json` out of the test folder, then restart. Sample records should appear.

* **Invalid file:** Replace the test file with invalid JSON, then restart. An empty list should appear and the log should record the load failure. Do not run commands before restoring the backup; a successful command saves over the file.
* **Old valid file:** Load AB3 data without tuition properties. The contact details should remain and the card should show `Lessons: Not recorded`.
* **Pre-lesson file:** Load a file whose students have `subjects`, `weeklyLessonSlot` and `hourlyRate`. The contact details load, but those properties are ignored and removed on the next save.

Each student can have any number of lessons, and each lesson has a subject, a weekly time slot and an hourly rate. See the [Developer Guide](DeveloperGuide.md#product-scope) for the plan and open decisions.

### Record or clear a schooling level
| Set or replace a level | `edit 1 level/Secondary 1` |
| Include a level when adding a student | Add `level/Primary 5` to the `add` command |

The card shows `Level: Primary 5` when a level is recorded. If none is recorded, the level line is hidden. Leave out `level/` to keep the existing level when editing. Changing a level keeps every other field unchanged, including lessons.

Levels must have 1 to 30 characters after the space cleanup below. Start with a letter or digit and include at least one letter. Use English letters `A-Z` or `a-z`, digits `0-9`, spaces and these symbols: `'`, `-`, `.`, `(`, `)`. Leading and trailing spaces or tabs are removed, and repeated spaces or tabs become one space. An empty `level/` clears the level with `edit`, but is invalid with `add`. Repeating `level/` in one command is invalid. Invalid input leaves the record unchanged.

### Find students by name or schooling level: `find`
Without `level/`, searches names for whole words, ignoring letter case. A student appears if any keyword matches; keyword order does not matter.
* `find alex david` matches names containing `Alex` or `David`.

Use `find level/TEXT` to search schooling levels, ignoring letter case. Partial matches are allowed: `find level/prim` matches `Primary 5`. Students without a level are excluded. Supply one non-empty `level/` value; it cannot be combined with name keywords.
Subject, phone and other fields are not searched.

Each student can have zero or more lessons. A lesson has a subject, a weekly time slot and an hourly rate, which are always present, and an optional mode (physical or virtual) and location. A student cannot have two identical lessons, but lessons with overlapping time slots are allowed. Lesson commands use the student's positive `STUDENT_INDEX` in the currently displayed list, including search results. They preserve all other student fields.
Subject, slot and rate are required; mode and location are optional. The new lesson is added to the end of the student's lessons.

* **Read:** Use `list` or `find` to display the student. Their card lists each lesson in order, for example `- Math, Wednesday 1.00pm-5.00pm, SGD 45.50/hour, Physical, at Clementi Library` (mode and location are shown only when recorded), or shows `Lessons: Not recorded` when there are none. The number of a lesson is its position in that list, starting from 1.

Supply at least one field. Omitted fields stay unchanged. To remove a recorded mode or location, give its prefix with nothing after it: `mode/` clears the mode and `location/` clears the location (see the examples below).
Removes only that lesson. Later lessons move up by one position.

* **Subject** (`subject/`): 1 to 40 characters after space cleanup. Start with a letter or digit and include at least one letter. Use English letters, digits, spaces and these symbols: `'`, `-`, `.`, `(`, `)`. Leading and trailing spaces are removed and repeated spaces become one. Subjects are compared ignoring letter case, so `Math` and `math` are the same subject.

* **Lesson slot** (`slot/`): `DAY START END` on a single day, such as `Wed 1.00pm 5.00pm`. Use a three-letter day (`Mon` to `Sun`), and times like `1.00pm` or `10.30am` with minute precision. Days and `am`/`pm` are not case-sensitive, so `wed 1.00PM 5.00PM` also works. The end must be later than the start on the same day; overnight lessons are not supported. The card shows the full day name, for example `Wednesday 1.00pm-5.00pm`.

* **Hourly rate** (`rate/`): an amount in SGD per hour. It must be non-negative and have at most two decimal places; `45`, `45.5` and `45.50` are valid. Currency symbols, negative amounts and scientific notation are invalid.
* **Mode** (`mode/`, optional): `physical` or `virtual`, not case-sensitive. The card shows `Physical` or `Virtual`.

* **Location** (`location/`, optional): 1 to 100 characters, such as an address, room or meeting link. Repeated spaces become one, and locations are compared ignoring letter case. It must not contain a word of letters followed by `/` (such as `rate/`), which is read as a prefix; `Blk 123/4` and `https://zoom.us/j/1` are fine.

* **Clearing mode and location:** only `lesson-edit` can clear them, by leaving the value empty, for example `lesson-edit 1 2 location/` or `lesson-edit 1 2 mode/ location/`. `lesson-add` rejects an empty `mode/` or `location/`, and `lesson-delete` accepts neither.

* Adding a lesson, or editing one so that it becomes identical to another of the same student's lessons, is rejected as a duplicate. Mode and location are part of a lesson's identity, so the same subject, slot and rate at a different location or mode is not a duplicate.
* A student index or lesson index that does not exist is rejected.

* Empty values (except an empty `mode/` or `location/` in `lesson-edit`, which clears the field), repeated prefixes, unknown prefixes and invalid values, such as a mode other than `physical` or `virtual`, are rejected. Any error leaves the record unchanged.
2. `lesson-add 1 subject/English slot/Mon 4.00pm 5.00pm rate/40 mode/virtual location/https://zoom.us/j/123` adds an online lesson with a meeting link.
3. `lesson-edit 1 2 rate/50` changes the English lesson's rate.
4. `lesson-edit 1 2 mode/physical location/Clementi Library` changes it to an in-person lesson at a new place.
5. `lesson-edit 1 2 location/` removes the location but keeps the mode. `lesson-edit 1 2 mode/ location/` removes both.
6. `lesson-delete 1 1` removes the Math lesson. English is now lesson 1.

The app saves automatically after each successfully executed command. Schooling levels, guardian contacts and lessons are saved with the contact details. Each student's lessons are stored as a `lessons` array, where every lesson has a `subject`, a `weeklyLessonSlot` and an `hourlyRate`, plus an optional `mode` (`PHYSICAL` or `VIRTUAL`) and `location`. Older files that stored a student's `subject`, `subjects`, `weeklyLessonSlot` or `hourlyRate` directly on the student still load, but those values are ignored and are lost the next time the app saves. Re-enter them with `lesson-add` or copy them into a `lessons` array first.
If saving fails, the app reports an error. The change may still appear on screen without being saved to disk.
Records are stored in `data/addressbook.json` under the folder where you start the app.

Close the app and back up the JSON file before editing it. Keep the existing file structure and valid field values.

StudentBook helps private tutors manage student contacts using typed commands. Records stay on the tutor's computer.

This development version lets you save student contacts, add, edit or clear subjects, a schooling level, a weekly lesson slot or an hourly rate, and find students by level. Separate guardian commands add, edit and remove one optional name and phone contact per student, displayed in the student list. See the [Developer Guide](DeveloperGuide.md#product-scope) for scope and feature owners.

The course expects peer review and values useful comments attached to specific code locations. It does not prescribe a universal number of reviewers or an identical depth for every change. In reviews, explain the concern and its effect, ask about intent when unclear, and suggest an alternative when useful. Keep comments civil, specific, and understandable to future readers. When CI fails, first identify which check, environment, and change caused it. Coverage warnings can be an informed exception when a part is unsuitable for automated testing or tests are deliberately deferred. Codecov targets can be adjusted; Codecov itself is not graded. This is not a blanket reason to ignore compilation failures, broken behavior, or style violations. Restore a useful passing CI state promptly. Occasional failures do not automatically incur a direct penalty; prolonged failures remove regression protection and can reveal separately penalized problems.

If local tests pass but a PR fails, compare OS behavior and reproduce the PR's merge with current `master`. PR CI tests the proposed combined state, not necessarily the exact standalone branch tested locally. If `master` changed after CI passed, synchronize and rerun before merging. File case, separators, locale/time assumptions, and platform-sensitive behavior deserve attention; do not assume a filesystem's case sensitivity solely from its OS name.

The course requires SE-EDU's **basic and intermediate Java rules**. Advanced Java rules, the Markdown guide, and Google's documentation style are optional. Checkstyle checks only part of the required standard. The live standard is the complete reference; read it when reviewing code rather than treating this reminder as exhaustive. [Course conventions](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/standardsAndConventions.html).

Java review reminders: use meaningful English names, lower-case packages, PascalCase types, camelCase members, uppercase underscore-separated constants, Boolean-sounding predicates, and plural collection names. Use four-space indentation, eight extra spaces for continuations, and a 120-character hard limit (110 preferred). Use braces, consistent explicit imports, narrow variable scope, and encapsulated fields. Keep layout and whitespace consistent. Document classes and public methods; exemptions include ordinary accessors, tests, and overrides whose inherited contract applies unchanged. Javadoc opens on its own line, starts a method summary with a third-person verb such as "Returns," and sits immediately above the declaration. Include useful parameter/return/exception details, with all parameters documented or none under the standard's omission rule. Use American English. [Complete Java standard](https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/intermediate.html).

Every commit needs an imperative, initially capitalized subject without a final period. Aim for 50 characters, with 72 as the hard limit; a meaningful scope/category prefix is allowed. A body is optional for this course. If present, separate it with a blank line, wrap at 72 characters, and use paragraphs explaining the change and its reason. More elaborate conventions are optional. [Git conventions](https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/git.html).

Choose tests by risk and usefulness. Manual GUI/system testing remains valuable. A useful strategy checks ordinary flows, invalid inputs, boundary cases, interactions, persistence, and regressions introduced by a change.

Early iterations may preserve existing tests without immediately adding new ones. Temporary disabling during volatile development or a draft PR is discussed as an option, with explicit risks: hidden regressions, accumulating test debt, and forgotten re-enablement. Removing tests that are not worth maintaining is also a tradeoff, not a free quality improvement. By final assessment, weak tests can cost marks through escaped bugs and lack of evidence of testing skill.

Code-quality assessment looks for sensible abstraction levels, manageable methods and nesting, little duplication (including tests), and appropriate use of exceptions, assertions, logging, and defensive programming. GUI automation is optional because maintaining it across desktop/CI environments is difficult. AB4 can be studied for TestFX examples, but cite reused AB4 code. Tests may be selectively enabled in environments where they work.

## Feature freeze: rule published in Week 10

Week 10 introduces the freeze that starts at the **v1.5 deadline**. The future weekly pages are tentative, so obtain the final start/end dates from their live instructions before acting. This section preserves the already-published mechanism, not a fixed Week 11/12 submission schedule. [Week 10 feature-freeze rules and FAQs](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/tp-w10.html).

Each member's functional-code changes during the freeze must stay within the greater of **15% of that person's final functional LoC or 150 lines**. Functional code is code files under `src/main`; blanks and comments in those files count. Test files, documentation, and non-code assets do not count in that category.

The numerator counts lines present in the final version, attributed to that member, that were added or edited during the freeze. Repeated edits to the same surviving line count once. Deletion does not add changed lines but can shrink the final denominator. Cosmetic refactoring still changes lines. Do not move code, alter attribution, or borrow a teammate's allowance to evade the rule. Legitimate help is allowed with honest attribution.

The published rules describe a five-percentage-point tolerance and a case-dependent penalty with a minimum of two marks beyond it. Plan to the stated allowance, not to the tolerance. The dashboards update periodically (about three hours); use the functional-code and freeze views and inspect anomalies rather than trusting a stale figure. Author annotations can affect automated attribution.

There is no separate categorical ban on a particular kind of edit in the published freeze rule, but new features are strongly discouraged. Prioritize fixes by user impact, confidence, and remaining allowance. Documented workarounds and lower-priority improvements can affect bug triage, but do not make an actual serious defect disappear. If a proposed fix crosses the allowance, compare the risks rather than automatically expanding scope; the rule notes that an individual bug penalty does not exceed two marks. Reverting a change before the final submission can remove that change from the freeze calculation.

Code quality is inspected manually and automatically. Required conventions, sensible abstraction levels, little duplication, and appropriate error handling/defensive measures matter. Effort is estimated for the whole product by peer testers and tutors, then allocated to members using team evaluations, tutor judgment, and Git evidence. The published baseline says a team effort rating above 5 with a roughly equal share should satisfy the effort bar. More LoC does not by itself earn higher marks.

UG/DG quality is evaluated as a whole, then individual contribution is assessed and cross-checked. A polished team document does not establish that every member contributed. Keep honest evidence of authorship and review.

The contribution scale is relative to an equal share: for a four-person team, equal share is one quarter; "equal share + 10%" means 1.10 times that quarter, not an additional ten percentage points of the whole project. Implementation, UG, and DG contributions are rated separately. The product-design rubric distinguishes a clear narrow audience, useful value, efficient typing-oriented interaction, and features that fit together. UG/DG comparisons to AB3 use four choices: significantly lower, slightly lower, similar, or higher quality.

For project management, aim to complete at least **75% of tasks on time**, use meaningful issues/owners/milestones/releases, follow the prescribed workflows, and leave buffers. PE measures testing, product evaluation, effort estimation, and the ability to report/respond to defects accurately. Tester credit and developer penalties are calculated separately; they are not a zero-sum exchange. Bugs in one's work affect different assessment components according to their nature. Developer testing considers **bug density**, not just raw bug count.

Tester marks are calibrated to how buggy the assigned product proves to be across its testers. If hardly any bugs are found collectively, more weight can be put on the tester's own developer-testing result. Full credit does not require discovering every defect and identifying the six objectively worst ones. Do honest focused testing and select the strongest reports you actually found.

Severity affects credit/penalty. Functionality, design, and documentation bugs affect different grade components; their testing credit is roughly comparable, so choose the correct type rather than trying to optimize labels. Penalties are divided equally among responsible assignees. Duplicate reports do not multiply the developer penalty, while different testers can receive credit for finding the same defect. A tester does not gain multiple credits for their own duplicates. Obvious defects can earn less credit. Incorrect rejection, severity reduction, or duplicate classification can hurt response-accuracy marks.

## Phase 1: scope, report format, and selection

Test the submitted JAR and the web-rendered UG/DG. The rest of the website, README, Markdown source, and code quality are not themselves PE documentation targets. Source inspection can help testing, but a code-quality concern needs an observable in-scope defect to become a PE report. Configuration/data files matter through supported behavior, including documented manual editing. Terminal output is lower-priority but can be a bug when misleading or alarming. Start with the manual-test appendix and expand into exploratory, system, and acceptance testing.

Each issue must be self-contained and report **one bug**. Include a specific title, setup/version/environment where relevant, reproducible steps, actual and expected results, and evidence of user impact. Put everything needed in the description: Phase 1 comments are not processed as part of the report. Do not use cross-issue links or sub-issues to bundle reports; IDs can change during transfer. Escape angle-bracket placeholders or put them in code formatting so GitHub does not hide them as HTML.
Use exactly one type and one severity label:
| `type.FunctionalityBug` | Implemented behavior does not work as it should |
| `type.FeatureFlaw` | A design choice or missing capability impairs the target user's task |
| `type.DocumentationBug` | Incorrect, missing, confusing, or badly presented UG/DG information |
| `severity.VeryLow` | Cosmetic/minor presentation issue without meaningful operational disruption |
| `severity.Low` | Minor issue or rare inconvenience; limited interference with normal work |
| `severity.Medium` | Meaningful occasional inconvenience, while the product can still be used |
| `severity.High` | Makes the product almost unusable for most intended users |

Use the live definitions, not this shorthand, for a borderline report. Explain both the chosen impact and why the next lower severity is insufficient. Prefer the lower severity when uncertain unless the evidence fits the higher one more closely. Missing severity defaults to Low; multiple severities lead to the lowest. Missing/multiple type labels can lead to an arbitrary type, so correct the metadata yourself.

Only reports/updates within the phase deadline count. Select **at most six** by leaving them open and closing the rest before the deadline; the highest-scoring **five** are graded. A report may be reopened before the cutoff. If more than six remain open, scripts prioritize severity, breaking ties by earlier issue number; excess reports are ignored. Select by impact, validity, and confidence, not bug type. Correct initial severity on an Accepted or NotInScope result can increase accuracy credit; the page gives an indicative 15–20%, not a guaranteed fixed formula.

Do not bundle numerous cosmetic defects under an extremely broad issue to evade the limit. If several distinct bugs are combined, developers may select one and discard the others. A valid defect remains valid even if the tester suggests the wrong fix or chooses the wrong type label.

Complete the assigned TEAMMATES evaluation; it is required and missing it can incur a penalty. Use the recovery-email facility if the link is missing. When the server is busy, wait several minutes instead of repeatedly reloading.

Evaluate product usefulness and cohesion for its stated user, especially efficient CLI use. Judge the UG's usefulness and the DG's value to future developers relative to the provided AB3 reference. The effort scale is 0–20, with implementing AB3 from scratch at 10 and a typical sufficient TP increment around 5. Exclude documentation, tests, and project-management work from this implementation-effort estimate, and do not adjust for team size yourself; the grading process handles that. Give sincere comments and concerns where requested rather than arbitrary ratings.

Received reports appear in the team's private course repository, `pe-<team-ID>`. Do not create replacement issues, transfer reports, or edit the original report title/body. Those actions can invalidate a response and leave the report treated as accepted. Closing/pinning reports for team organization is allowed in this phase; closed reports are still processed. Contact staff for a report assigned to the wrong product.

Assign each report to the member(s) responsible for that feature/section. No assignee, or assigning every member, counts as **unassigned**. No more than **50% of all received reports** may be unassigned. Exceeding that brings a **20% tax on each person's total bug penalty** under the current rules. All reports count toward that ratio regardless of response; duplicate reports inherit the original's assignees and still count individually. Responsibility for a report is separate from scheduling its fix; coordinate any code changes through the team workflow and applicable freeze rules.
Choose exactly one response label and ensure type/severity are correct even when disputing the report:
| `response.Accepted` | It is a valid defect that should be addressed in the current product |
| `response.NotInScope` | It is a valid improvement, but justifiably lower-priority than the work delivered |
| `response.NotApplicable` | The alleged problem is not a valid defect; behavior is correct or the claim is mistaken |
| `response.CannotReproduce` | Reasonable repeated attempts with the available information cannot reproduce it |
| `response.IssueUnclear` | The report lacks enough understandable information to determine the issue |

Missing or multiple response labels default to Accepted. Do not confuse NotInScope with NotApplicable: the former acknowledges a valid potential improvement. Do not reject a real defect for a wrong label or incorrect proposed remedy; correct the label and explain which remedy is appropriate. Reporters cannot participate in an informal clarification conversation during this anonymous phase, so do not rely on asking questions in ordinary comments.

Put the developer explanation in **one comment starting with `# T`**, at most **500 words**. The latest matching comment is used. A comment is required when lowering severity, choosing a non-Accepted response, marking a duplicate, or changing type. Accepting entirely unchanged needs no justification. A type change needs the response comment but does not itself require a justification under the current instructions. Explain all disputed decisions clearly, using titles rather than unstable cross-repository issue numbers.

Unjustified rejection or downgrading is weak evidence if challenged. Moderators choose between supported positions; do not start with an exaggerated bargaining position in the hope of meeting halfway. Use a separate `# U` comment only for unprofessional conduct, not for an inaccurate or unpersuasive report.

Use GitHub **sub-issues**: make duplicate reports children of one representative original report. Keep the structure flat; do not create chains of duplicates. The original's response/type/severity/assignees control the children. Each child's `# T` explanation must state why it is a duplicate. The tester receives both relevant explanations, so put any inherited severity reduction's rationale where it will be visible.

Reports are duplicates when they concern the same defect or a common underlying problem that cannot be fixed independently. Similar symptoms alone are insufficient. Two unrelated typos that can be corrected independently are not automatically duplicates. If the duplicate classification is overturned, the inherited classification can still matter under the stated process, so choose and justify it carefully.

Recommended team process: set an internal responsibility-assignment deadline, assign remaining reports by agreement, draft responses, and have teammates check them before the external deadline. Accurate fair responses matter more than reducing the accepted count.

Wait for the official announcement before acting; seeing script comments appear does not mean the transfer is finished. Responses are copied back to the tester's private repository. Read the report's listed aspects that may be challenged. The permitted objections are response, lowered severity, and duplicate status; **bug type is not an objection category**.
If you agree, no counter-response is needed. Otherwise, add a separate comment for each disputed aspect, **at most 500 words each**, starting with the exact applicable heading:

For `# R`, explicitly say if the requested outcome is NotInScope; otherwise Accepted is assumed. Additional evidence may be provided, but it carries less weight than information included in the original report, especially if the developer could not reasonably infer it. Explain why the response is wrong instead of merely repeating the report.

Do not change the original title/body/labels, create/edit/delete repository labels, or close issues in this phase. Reopen an accidentally closed issue. Edit the existing objection before the deadline rather than creating multiple versions. No objection means agreement; optional agreement checkboxes do not replace a required objection.

To withdraw an objection, delete it or remove its special heading. Hiding it or checking an agreement box does **not** retract it. There is little value in disputing severity/duplicate status after agreeing to a response that earns no bug credit. NotInScope is different: severity still affects the value of the accepted improvement and the accuracy calculation.

The current rules offer an accuracy amnesty for agreeing with the developer's response, not for an incorrect original severity. An unsuccessful objection can reduce accuracy, particularly when better information was available. Correct final response/severity judgments can improve credit; published bonus percentages are indicative and should be reread before relying on them.

Tutors adjudicate disputes using the report, developer explanation, and tester objection. Students normally take no further action. Staff will not pre-decide whether a proposed report is a bug or assign its severity during the assessment; those are assessed judgments. General procedural questions can go through the designated channel with relevant context.
## Triage principles for design and implementation
Read the full [PE triage guidelines](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/tp-pe.html) for a contested case. These points should also guide development before PE:
- **Inherited defects:** AB3 behavior is not automatically exempt. The team owns its delivered product.

- **Reproduction:** make a reasonable attempt to understand the issue even if steps are imperfect but screenshots/context reveal it. OS-specific defects are valid on supported systems; affected reach can influence severity. A transferred broken image may need staff assistance rather than instant rejection.

- **Scope:** NotInScope needs a credible priority/resource argument relative to work already done. A known limitation or coming-soon note is evidence, not immunity. Essential usability or an obviously better design achievable at similar effort is difficult to defer credibly. If equally persuasive subjective design arguments remain, the course's feature-design FAQ favors the developer.

- **Long/extreme inputs:** deliberate sabotage alone can fall outside scope, but ordinary mistakes must not crash the app, corrupt data, or make it unusable. Apply the same principle to numeric overflow. Reasonable length limits are allowed; limits must fit actual users. Clipping can be cosmetic or serious depending on information lost.

- **Validation:** accepting useful real-world inputs often matters more than enforcing a programmer's narrow format. Warn rather than block when flexibility is safe; handle harmful invalid input properly. A parser delimiter is not by itself a sufficient reason to exclude common legitimate names without considering impact.

- **Duplicates and search:** case/whitespace variants can represent the same entity. Warn about near matches where appropriate, allow sensible user choice, and explain detection limits. Case sensitivity should reflect the represented domain. Search should help the user recover likely results; the guideline's OR-versus-AND example is context-specific, not a command to rewrite every search.

- **Commands:** optimize frequent tasks for fast typing with memorable syntax; unnecessary case sensitivity, long keywords, or awkward characters can be feature flaws. Useful short aliases plus longer memorable forms can help.

- **Errors:** identify the actual problem and remedy where feasible. A generic message can be inadequate even when technically true. Distinguish invalid values from malformed input, or give an accurate combined message where further differentiation is justifiably lower-priority.
- **Manual data editing:** support at least AB3's promise that correctly edited files work. Stronger UG promises must be met. The human-editable storage constraint still applies.

- **Undocumented behavior:** hidden unreleased work may be outside the released scope if users are unlikely to encounter it. An exposed unfinished feature, or a useful non-obvious feature with missing instructions, can be a bug. Obvious intuitive behavior need not always have a lengthy UG entry.

Broken links can be Low or Medium depending on their effect. Formatting, spacing, inconsistent alignment, or unreadable diagrams can be bugs even if a determined reader could work around them; minor presentation issues are usually VeryLow. An obvious typo, including text in the UI, is normally a VeryLow documentation bug, while an inconsequential grammatical preference may be NotInScope.

UML must use correct relevant course notation. Harmless extra tool decorations are different from misleading notation. Consistent omission of optional notation can be acceptable; intentional abstraction should be clear, whereas accidental omissions that misrepresent the design are defects. Do not assume zooming excuses tiny text. Incorrect requirements, missing important interaction cases, and unrealistic/unmet NFR claims can also be documentation defects or design flaws depending on what needs changing.

A UG need not contain every validation corner case when the product informs the user adequately. Conversely, claims must match behavior and important limitations must be disclosed. Choose bug type by the needed correction: change behavior/design for a product defect, or correct the guide for a documentation error. Neither a misleading guide nor a poor design is excused merely because the two agree.

The grading checklist also flags too few or too many visuals/examples, visuals disconnected from the explanation, repetitive content, unexplained audience-specific jargon, and descriptions that are too short or unnecessarily long. DG-specific risks include non-intuitive architecture symbols, indiscriminate double-headed arrows, low-level detail in an architecture view, an unsuitable diagram type, non-UML diagrams where UML would serve equally well, excessive code extracts, mismatched user-story parts, missing important stories/use cases, bad step numbering, unnecessary UI details in use cases, missing extensions, and vague or implausible NFRs. Check whether each glossary entry actually helps the intended reader.
